note: The field journal (docs 13, 15): the words it writes and the numbers that shape them. order: the living things with pages, in page order. Each species: name and icon (src/ui/icons), riddle (shown before it has been seen), amount ([at least this many plants, words] steps; a cover plant (kind cover: grass, rushes) uses its share of the dry ground instead, or with amountBy area the square meters it covers), place and compass (where words: compass false skips the side of the island), none (after it has gone), clause words (flowering, dormant, spreading, receding), stages (what tapping one says, by growth stage: seed, sprout, young, mature, flowering, dormant), seasons (what each season box says: grow per season, flower, dormant), likes (lines learned when one of the learn triggers happens: seen, spread, flower, lost:drown, lost:seed, refused:<need>, grass:flooded), gives (a pencil line until the when trigger, then the ink line), notes (the lines the journal writes). trend: a species is spreading when it has gained at least max(upMin, upShare x then) plants over trend hours, receding when it has lost at least max(downMin, downShare x then). where: spreadOut is the mean distance from the plants' middle, as a share of the island's radius, past which they are all around the island; centerShare is how close to the island's middle counts as the middle. notesKept: notes the journal keeps; pageNotes: notes on a species page. islandNote: how long a note stays on the island (showS), the gap between two (gapS) and how many may wait (queue). identify: how near a tap must be to a plant (radiusM), how long the card stays (showS), and the size of the breathing ring around what was tapped (ringM for a full-grown plant, smaller for young ones; grassRingM on grass; its timing is in recipes/world/growth.json marks). arrivedHours: plants seen within this many hours of the journal starting were here when you arrived. J1.5: each species also has plural (for the story lines), field (field notes: natural history lines learned like likes, by triggers that include dormant, woke and moment:<id>) and fieldHint (the pencil line while some are still to learn). story: the lines of 'your island's story' ({Plural}, {plural} and {date} are filled in; peak shows when the count has fallen under peakShare of its best). moments: four frames per page by kind (plant, cover for grass and rushes, ground in journal-island.json), each filled the first time you tap that thing at that moment: flower (in flower), summer, winter, rain (rain at least rainAt), mist (at least mistAt), dawn and dusk (hours of the day, inclusive start, exclusive end), frost (a winter dawn); note is the line written. showMe: how long (showS) the ring and card stay after a page's Show me rings the example nearest the middle of your view (the camera does not move). S6a, animals: a creature (kind creature: frogs) is known only once you find one yourself (tap it, or watch it from close by; recipes/species/frog.json find), never just because it is on the island; until then its page shows the riddle, or the latest of its hints whose journal flag is set (frogs:right when the pond is right for them, frogs:sign after the first sign). Its notes come in two voices: the unseen ones speak of something (a sign, rings on the water), never naming it; the others once it is known. A swarm (kind swarm: midges) is known by itself, like a plant, at the first dusk (seenAt.hours) that at least seenAt.m2 square meters hold seenAt.share of a full cloud; its amount is in those square meters. seenAt.drawn: whether the island draws the swarm yet; until it does (S6b), midges stay a pencil ? and nothing names them, because the journal only tells what you could see. card: what a tap on one says. foundLine: its story's first line. The animals' moments are moments.creature.

reveal._doc: The reveal on return (docs/02, src/world/journal/reveal-plan.js) shows its notes best first: by the first class whose kinds hold the note's kind (doc 02's order), then newer first; kinds not listed come last. Kinds are shared by every species, so a new plant or animal ranks by the kinds of its notes.

grass.name: Grass

field.text: Grass grows from the base of each blade, so it recovers quickly when it is grazed or trodden.
Its roots need air: standing water drowns them in a day or two.
Rain soaks into a meadow instead of running off, because the roots hold the soil open.
On cold dawns, frost whitens the tip of every blade.
By the water grass grows tall and dark; on the dry rise it is shorter and cures to straw in late summer.

rushes.name: Rushes and sedges

field.text: Rushes and sedges are grass-like plants of wet ground. They grow in tight tussocks.
In summer small brown flower tufts sprout near the top of the stems.
Their stems are full of soft pith, which carries air down to roots in the soaked mud.
The stems stay standing through winter, brown at the tips, and frost silvers them at dawn.

reeds.name: Reeds

field.text: Their roots knit the soft bank together, so the water's edge keeps its shape.
One clump becomes many: new shoots rise from roots creeping under the mud.
Each brown head is packed with thousands of tiny seeds, every one with its own fluff to fly on.
In winter the dry stalks stand on, and small creatures shelter among them from the wind.
Rain runs down the blades and into the mud around their feet.

lilies.name: Water lilies

field.text: Their pads float, but each one rises on a long stalk from roots anchored in the mud below.
The flowers open in the morning sun and close again toward evening.
Raindrops bead and roll on the waxy pads without wetting them.
In winter they rest as thick roots in the mud, waiting for the water to warm.
Shade from the pads keeps the water beneath them cool.

iris.name: Yellow flag iris

field.text: Its roots help clean the water that seeps through the bank.
It spreads by thick roots that creep just under the surface.
Each flower lasts only a day or two, but a clump opens them one after another for weeks.
The leaves die back in winter, but the roots stay alive under the soil.
At dusk the yellow flags seem to glow after the green has gone grey.

thrift.name: Sea thrift

field.text: Its tight cushion keeps the salt wind from drying it out.
Each pompom is many tiny papery flowers, packed together.
Its seeds ride the wind and only take where the ground is salty.
Rain and sea spray alike bead on its narrow leaves.
It stays green all winter, low and hunched against the cold.

field.text: Common frogs hide in cover by day and come out to hunt at dusk.
A frog's skin has to stay wet, so it never strays far from the water.
At dusk the males call, each one waiting for a gap before he calls again.
In winter they sleep in the soft mud at the bottom of the pond.

midges.name: Midges
midges.riddle: Something tiny might dance over the reeds on warm evenings.

field.text: Most midges don't bite. They dance in swarms over a marker, such as a reed tip.
Their young grow in the mud and still water under the reeds.
A swarm is mostly males, waiting for a female to fly into it.
Rain and wind send them down into the reeds until it passes.
